ï»¿**COMMENTS**
This composite source straddles a segment of the transpressional structures that deform the off-shore foreland in front of the external front of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt (SFTB). The SFTB forms the backbone of mainland Sicily and is part of the Maghrebian-Apennines orogenic belt forming the broad central-western Mediterranean collisional plate boundary. The leading edge of this thrust system crops out on-shore in its eastern portion between Gela and Catania, this section being confined to the east by the structures related to the subduction system of the Ionian basin, and in its western portion between Capo Granitola and Sciacca. In its central section it follows a broad southerly convex arch running for most of its length off-shore the southern Sicilian coast (Gela Nappe). In western Sicily, the general trend of the Plio-Quaternary SFTB external thrust front gradually turns to a NE-SW/NNE-SSW strike forming a northward recess around the Saccense Meso-Cenozoic carbonate platform. This front eventually crosses the Sicily Channel along the Adventure Thrust Front (ATF), thus connecting with the thrust fronts outcropping on-land in Tunisia. Off-shore the southern Sicily coast, to the east of the ATF, two N-S trending transpressional fault systems cut across the foreland faults, forming the Capo Granitola (CGFS) and Sciacca (SFS) fault systems (Ferranti et al., 2019). The latter, also known as the Belice-Sciacca Wrench Fault System (Argnani et al., 1986), is interpreted to separate two sectors of the Sicily Channel rift zone. The Sicilian-Maghrebian fold-and-thrust belt developed since early Miocene times in the framework of the ca. N-S directed Africa-Europe plate convergence and deformed rocks mostly belonging to the northern African paleomargin. This is characterized by carbonate platforms and interposed deep basins (Pelagian domain), involving in the deformation Neogene-Quaternary foredeep deposits along the external fronts. Geological and geophysical subsurface data show that in western Sicily the SFTB is made up of two superposed structural levels: the shallower, thin-skinned one composed of thrust sheets involving deep-water rocks, overthrusted during the Miocene on the deeper one, that in turn deforms the shallow-water platform carbonates of the Trapanese and Saccense units. From the late Miocene (Messinian), the lower level was deformed by deep-seated thrust ramps associated with long wavelength anticlines that passively refolded the upper structural level (Oldow et al., 1990; Avellone et al., 2010; Catalano et al., 2013).
The most recent GPS solutions for the broad Sicily area, due to a denser network of stations, supply a greater detail for the area included between the Hyblean foreland and the Sicilian-Maghrebian chain in eastern Sicily (e.g., Devoti et al., 2017). At the regional scale, GPS data highlight an average Nâ€“S pattern of convergence across the outer fronts of the on-land sectors of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system, in agreement with geological evidence of their recent activity testified by the deformation of Plio-Quaternary foredeep deposits and south of the Mt. Etna volcano, of late Pleistocene-Holocene marine and fluvial deposits.
Historical and instrumental catalogues show that in Sicily and surrounding areas the most important seismic events are located in few distinct sectors, including the Belice area, the Southern Tyrrhenian Sea offshore the northern Sicily coast, the Nebrodi and Peloritani mountain ranges, the Mount Etna and the Hyblean regions, while only scattered and minor seismicity is observed in central Sicily (Caltanissetta Basin) and in the Sicily Channel. In western Sicily, the only destructive earthquakes occurred during the 1968 seismic sequence, with a mainshock on 15 January 1968 (Mw 6.41 from Rovida et al., 2021) that had its mesoseismal area in the Valle del Belice. The sequence, whose core includes at least three major events, spanned from 14 to 25 January (e.g., Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Azzaro et al., 2020), and lasted until September 1968 (De Panfilis and Marcelli, 1968). Different focal solutions have been proposed in the literature for this sequence, including compressional (McKenzie, 1972) or strike-slip mechanisms (Anderson and Jackson, 1987; Gasparini et al., 1980, 1982; Neri et al., 2005). According to the latter group of investigators, the 1968 sequence may have occurred by right-lateral/compressional slip along NNW-SSE striking planes. In both cases, the average P-axis is low-dipping and nearly N-S trending. Accordingly, there are two fault models proposed in the literature: a) N-S right-lateral faulting along a lithospheric transcurrent fault system, which would extend from the Sicily Channel to the southern Sicilian coast, or to the northern Sicilian coast (San Vito Lo Capo - Sciacca shear zone, SVCS; Di Stefano et al., 2015) and would have allowed the differential flexural retreat of the Pelagian foreland, or b) reverse faulting along the E-W striking thrust front.
More to the west, with respect to the Belice area, the 7 June 1981, Mw 4.9, Mazara del Vallo earthquake was characterized by a reverse mechanism with a nearly N-S P-axis (Pondrelli et al, 2006) further testifying the activity of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system.
In addition to the historical and instrumental events listed in the Italian catalogues, a detailed and systematic critical analysis of the archaeological data in the Selinunte area showed that at least two seismic events struck the Selinunte temples causing their collapse (e.g., Guidoboni et al., 2002; Bottari et al., 2009). These seismic events, dated to a period between the fourth and third centuries B.C. and between the fourth and sixth century A.D., respectively, are currently not included in the Italian seismic catalogues.
To the SW of the Belice area, the SFTB front follows a NE-SW trending thrust fault array that straddles across the coastline and is composed by several segments showing geodetic and geologic evidence of active deformation (Barreca et al., 2014, 2020; Ferranti et al., 2019, 2021). The northern, on-land segment corresponds with an up to 60 m high morphological scarp, which is the fore-limb of a broad fold involving Lower Pleistocene sediments and cm-scale reverse displacement of an early Bronze-Hellenistic age road. It is marked by a sharp gradient in Differential SAR interferometry and GPS velocity fields. Inversion of fault slip-lineation data from structures displacing the archaeological remains yielded a N110Â°E shortening axis, consistent with the geodetic shortening direction estimated from GPS differential velocities. In the off-shore, the southern segments of the SFTB run along the Adventure Thrust Front, while, slightly to the east, the foreland is crossed by the transpressional faults and folds of the CGFS and SFS, which show on Sparker seismic profiles folding of Late Pleistocene-Holocene deposits and out-of-syncline thrust splays cutting the sea-floor. This sector of the Sicilian-Maghrebian thrust system may be tentatively correlated to the seismic events that induced the destruction of Selinunte temples due to their proximity to the archaeological site (Hinzen et al., 2018), however, up to now there is no conclusive evidence on where the causative earthquakes were really generated.
We believe that this sector of the Apennine-Maghrebide thrust system is characterised by infrequent moderate earthquakes generated on blind segments of the SFTB thrust system or on segments of the off-shore transpressional Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems.
This Composite Source belongs to the southern section of the SFS, and its strike was taken from the general orientation of the transpressional tectonic structures off-shore Capo San Marco mapped using marine geophysical data and bathymetric data. The dip was inferred from 1) regional geological considerations concerning the fault system and 2) the interpretation of seismic lines. The rake was assumed to represent left-lateral transpression based on general geodynamic considerations, the interpretation of the geological structures mapped in the off-shore and the direction of the regional compressive strain field derived from geodetic data. The minimum depth was based on the geometry of the faults underlying the off-shore folds as derived from seismic lines, while the maximum depth was inferred by geometrical considerations concerning the depth at which active thrusting is rooted. Slip rate was inferred from regional geodynamic data.

pictures.t: Geodynamic map of the central Mediterranean area
pictures.c: Geodynamic map of the central Mediterranean area with simplified trace of the active fault systems dorming the Pelagian foreland and rates of late Pleistocene uplift as derived from marine terrace inner margin elevations (from Ferranti et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Geological map and cross-sections of south-western Sicily
pictures.c: Geologic and tectonic map of south-western Sicily (panel A) and geological cross-sections (panel B) showing the geometry of the outer fronts of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt south of the Belice area. The deposits of the lower Pleistocene Marsala Fm. registered the most recent compressional activity along the Castevetrano-Campobello scarp (from Ferranti et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Pleistocene marine terraces in south-western Sicily
pictures.c: Panel (A) shows in map view the inner margins of Pleistocene marine terraces and the innermost position in outcrop of the deposits of the Marsala Fm. along a ca. 100 km long stretch of the south-western Sicily coastline. The elevation of the inner margins is plotted in the section shown in panel (B) together with the topography to highlight the morphological expression of the frontal folds of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt (from Ferranti et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Linear regressions of inner margin elevations of marine terraces in south-western Sicily
pictures.c: Panel (A) shows the inner margin elevations of middle-upper Pleistocene terraces and the maximum elevation of the deposits of the Marsala Fm. along the coast of south-western Sicily, with their linear regressions, highlighting the regional tectonic uplift, with rates increasing eastward. Panel (B) shows the differential elevation profiles, together with the profile of the line of sight mean velocity obtained from InSAR data, to emphasize the local signals due to the growth of the outer folds of the Sicilian Fold and Thrust Belt (from Ferranti et al., [2021])

pictures.t: Structural and geological map of the Sicily channel
pictures.c: Simplified structural and geological map of the Sicily channel off-shore south-western Sicily, showing the fault trace of the Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems, together with bathymetry and isobaths of the base of the Pliocene-Quaternary sediments (from Ferranti et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems interpreted by Ferranti et al. [2019]
pictures.c: Structural map of the Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems derived from the interpretation of marine geophysical data (from Ferranti et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Seismic profiles across the Capo Granitola Fault System
pictures.c: Interpreted high-penetration multichannel seismic profiles across the northern segment of the Capo Granitola Fault System showing the deep geometry of the transpressional structure (from Ferranti et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Seismic profiles across the Sciacca Fault System
pictures.c: Interpreted high-penetration multichannel seismic profiles across the northern (a) and southern (b) segments of the Sciacca Fault System showing the deep geometry of the transpressional structure (from Ferranti et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Depth-converted profiles across the Sciacca Fault System
pictures.c: Depth-converted high-resolution single-channel profiles across the northern segment of the Sciacca Fault System showing the shallow expression of the transpressional structure (from Ferranti et al., [2019])

pictures.t: Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems interpreted by Civile et al. [2018]
pictures.c: Simplified structural map of the Capo Granitola and Sciacca fault systems and distribution of the magmatic manifestations in the Sicily Channel (from Civile et al., [2018])

pictures.t: Profile FASTMIT-05 across the Capo Granitola Fault System
pictures.c: Depth-migrated multichannel seismic profile FASTMIT-05 across the northern segment of the Capo Granitola Fault System (from Civile et al., [2018])
